analysis.one_liner: Lets investors sue brokers and advisers in court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill 27-23 in November 2021, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for broker-dealers and investment advisers to write contracts forcing customers into arbitration or banning class action lawsuits, and would bar companies from mandating arbitration in their governing documents. Customers who have already been forced to sign such clauses could have them voided, though they could still choose arbitration voluntarily. The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee on a narrow 27-23 vote in November 2021 but never received a vote from the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: Retail investors who would otherwise have to sign away their right to sue. Someone defrauded by a broker or adviser could take the case to court or join a class action instead of being confined to arbitration chosen by the firm.

how_it_helps.text: Bars broker-dealers, funding portals, municipal securities dealers, and investment advisers from agreements that mandate arbitration, restrict forum choice, or block class action claims.
Prohibits securities issuers from mandating arbitration of shareholder disputes in bylaws or shareholder contracts, enforced through listing and registration rules.
Voids prohibited clauses in agreements already signed before enactment, while preserving arbitrations already underway.
Leaves investors free to choose arbitration if they judge it the better option; the bill targets only clauses imposed before a dispute arises.

analysis.who_pays: Brokerage firms and investment advisers lose their ability to force disputes into arbitration and shield themselves from class actions, and face greater court exposure when customers sue. Public companies lose the option of mandating arbitration of shareholder disputes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brokers, investment advisers, and public companies

drawbacks.text: The securities industry's arbitration forum is comparatively quick and low-cost for small individual claims; without arbitration mandates, some small investors may find litigation slower and more expensive, so a small-dollar dispute could become impractical to pursue.
Firms would face new litigation exposure and costs, some of which could be passed along to customers through fees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For investors with real losses, restoring the choice between court and arbitration outweighs the cost, since firms currently pick the forum in advance and block class actions in the fine print. The main cost falls on financial firms that lose that shield, and the main risk is that small individual claims become costlier to pursue in court.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Financial Services Committee 27-23 in November 2021, then sat without a floor vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced April 16, 2021 by Rep. Bill Foster with seven Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
On November 16, 2021, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill to be reported in the nature of a substitute, amended, by a recorded vote of 27 to 23.
No further action was taken; the bill was never reported to the full House and received no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and public companies keep the ability to force customers and shareholders into pre-agreed arbitration and to bar class actions. Retail investors retain no new recourse in court.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brokers and advisers who kept forced arbitration

for.name: Rep. Bill Foster
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through committee.

for.name: 7 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Maloney, Meeks, Casten, Velazquez, Garcia, Schakowsky, and Dean.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Convened the November 2021 markup at which the committee approved the bill 27-23.

against.name: 23 House Financial Services Committee members
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported in the 27-23 committee vote.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote after committee approval.

against.name: Securities industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory arbitration bans, arguing their arbitration forum serves small investors efficiently.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all seven cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee vote was narrow at 27-23, suggesting the vote broke largely along party lines though the record does not list individual votes.

industries.note: They would lose the ability to require customers to arbitrate disputes and to waive class actions, facing court claims instead. Their interest in keeping that shield runs against investors' interest in choosing their own forum.
They could no longer mandate arbitration of shareholder disputes in bylaws or contracts, enforced through listing and registration rules, which would expose them to more shareholder lawsuits.

Lifting bans on class actions opens a pool of potential securities cases. This gain runs alongside investors' gain in court access, though individual small-dollar claims may still be hard to litigate.
